$comment: Single source of truth for every marketing fact that appears on more than one page.
Why this exists: the static pages in public/ are hand-authored HTML with no template
layer, so a price or trial length changes in one place and silently rots in 130 others.
That happened three times (llms.txt pricing URL, an admit-rate placeholder, and the trial
length, which was wrong on every single static page while the app itself was correct).
It then happened a fourth time, which is why `retiredPrices` and the jsonld-offer-price
rule now exist. Weekly billing was retired in the app and in Stripe on 2026-08-30, but
120 static pages kept a JSON-LD offer of "price": "2.99" and the landing page still
opened on a Weekly tab. Visible copy had been swept; structured data had not, because
JSON-LD carries the amount and the interval in separate fields and the original
price-interval-pairing rule only ever looked at prose like "$2.99/month".
The values here are NOT the runtime source of truth for billing. lib/server/trialPlan.js
is, and it stays that way because it is revenue-critical and independently tested.
scripts/check-facts.mjs asserts this file agrees with it, so marketing copy cannot drift
away from what Stripe actually charges without failing the build.
To change a fact: edit it here, run `npm run facts:sync`, commit the result.
To verify nothing has drifted: `npm run facts:check` (also runs as part of `npm test`).
$retiredComment: Amounts we used to charge and no longer sell. Any appearance of one of these in a
customer-facing file is a bug: it advertises a price Stripe will not honour.
Dropping `week` from plans above is necessary but not sufficient. allowedPriceIntervals()
only inspects amounts it recognises as ours, so once 2.99 stopped being one of our
prices the checker would have silently reclassified "$2.99/wk" as a competitor quote
and skipped it. Listing retired amounts explicitly closes that hole.
Verified 2026-08-31 that none of these collide with a competitor price quoted on any
comparison page: Chegg $15.95/mo, Course Hero $39.95/mo and Wolfram Alpha $7.99/mo are
the quoted competitors and none of them match.
$audienceComment: Real audience numbers. These exist because the static pages carried a fabricated
"500,000+ students" stat on 12 pages, a "50K+" stat on 2 more, and a
"4.8/5 from 2,000+ reviews" proof item on 5. None of those numbers were ever real.
`users` is the actual registered-user count (1,500+ as of 2026-10-30, per Ryan).
Express it as `usersPhrase` / `usersStat`. "Thousands" was used briefly and retired:
There is NO rating and there are NO reviews: the iOS app is not on the App Store yet.
`appStoreRating` stays null until a real store listing has one. Do not print a star
rating, a review count, or star glyphs next to a number anywhere until then.
The ONLY real testimonials are the five in the index.html marquee (Andy G., Danny K.,
Charlotte B., Gavin D., Alex G.). Every other named student quote on the site was
invented and has been removed. Reuse those five; never write a new one.
`followers` is the social following (TikTok), which is where the 30,000+ community
number comes from. It is NOT a user count. Never attach it to a label like
"students using StudyEdge AI" -- that converts a true number into a false one.
retiredAudienceClaims lists the exact fabricated strings. scripts/facts.mjs fails the
build if any of them reappears in a customer-facing file. Entries must be unambiguous
self-claims: "400,000+" is deliberately absent because UNISA genuinely enrolls that
many and best-study-app-for-unisa-students.html quotes it as a fact about the school.
$competitorPricesComment: Competitor prices that collide with one of our amounts at a different interval.
price-interval-pairing assumed any amount it did not recognise as ours belonged to a
competitor and could be skipped. The inverse case was never handled: a competitor
charging OUR amount at an interval we do not sell it at. That stayed invisible while
the checker ignored public/blog/, and surfaced the moment blog posts came into scope --
GoodNotes 6 really is $9.99/year and Notability really is $14.99/year, which collide
with Pro monthly ($9.99) and Unlimited monthly ($14.99).
Only add an entry after confirming the competitor genuinely charges that amount at
that interval. Each entry is a hole in the price checker, so keep the list short.
